description_full: Workday, Inc. provides enterprise cloud applications in the United States and internationally. The company offers a suite of financial management applications to maintain accounting information; manage financial processes, such as payables and receivables; identify real-time financial, operational, and management insights; perform financial consolidation; reduce time-to-close; promote internal control and auditability; and achieve consistency across finance operations. It also provides spend management solutions that help organizations to streamline supplier selection and contract management, build and execute sourcing events, such as requests for proposals, and manage indirect spend; expense management solutions to submit and approve expenses; and a suite of human capital management applications that enables HR teams to hire, onboard, pay, develop, reskill, and provide employee experiences. In addition, the company offers planning applications. Further, it provides supply chain and inventory solutions to healthcare organizations; solutions to manage the end-to-end student and faculty lifecycle; Workday Extend for customers and their developers to build custom applications. The company serves the professional and business services, financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, media, education, government, technology, media, retail, and hospitality industries. It sells its solutions through its direct sales organization. The company was formerly known as North Tahoe Power Tools, Inc. and changed its name to Workday, Inc. in July 2005. Workday, Inc. was incorporated in 2005 and is headquartered in Pleasanton, California.

financial_summary: Workday, Inc. is a large-cap technology business with a $47.3B market cap on $9.6B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +15% over the past three years and +23% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +3.9pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $2.8B in free cash flow — roughly 29 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 4.24× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage runs at 6.3×.

Management returns a meaningful 6.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and stock-based comp at 17% of revenue is silent dilution an owner has to account for, and insiders hold 2.1% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 17% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 17% below the high.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $156 (margin of safety -26%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 73%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $113 to $224 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Technology peers: cheaper on P/FCF 17.0 vs 26.1, richer on P/E 40.0 vs 27.4 and EV/EBITDA 29.2 vs 17.1 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 37 covering analysts target $209 on average, 7% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 20.1% annual cash-flow growth, 5pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.9%, so growth at these returns destroys value.
It converts 29% of revenue into free cash flow, or 12% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 4.24x.
ROE of 9% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.3x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 14pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 28.0% of revenue on R&D and 17.0% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $2.5B (5% of market cap).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 15.4% over 3 years, 17.2% over 5 years and 23.4% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 18%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 22.3% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (1.7% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.1%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (60 sales, net $150.6M sold).
It returns 6.1% a year to shareholders (6.1% in buybacks).
people: With about 20,896 employees, each generates about $457K of revenue, 1.2x the Technology median, and revenue has grown 28.9% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $133K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $3.9M (9x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (10/10, lower is better).
